Treatment Options
Observation/bracing/pain management
Observation or activity modifications are used in patients with very small lesions or advanced
disease in whom prior treatment attempts failed.
Functional bracing can be used in the spine, upper extremity, and distal lower extremity.
Pain management is used in all symptomatic patients.
Nonopioids: NSAIDs, acetaminophen, tricyclic antidepressants, gabapentin, muscle
relaxants, steroids
Opioids
A bowel program is necessary to prevent severe constipation.
Involvement of the palliative medicine team may be instrumental in balancing the adverse
effects of pain medication regimens.


Treatment Options
Observation is a viable treatment option for lesions that are asymptomatic (or mildly
symptomatic) and small or associated with low risk of impending fracture. These
patients should be appropriately educated on the presence of the metastatic lesion and
on symptoms of impending fracture, primarily worsening pain. Patients can be followed
via serial radiographs at a regular frequency based on clinical suspicion of potential
progression. Functional bracing may be used to promote nondisplaced fracture healing,
function, and comfort, particularly for stable lesions of the spine, upper extremity
(humeral shaft), and distal lower extremity (tibia/ankle/foot). Some anatomic locations in
which pathologic fractures occur, including the ischium, pubic rami, sacroiliac areas, and
scapulae, usually do not require surgical management. Observation also may be the best
treatment option for patients with very advanced disease in whom surgical treatment
may only cause additional morbidity or be considered futile. In these scenarios,
palliation in the form of pain management and activity modifications, with or without
functional bracing, is in the best interest of the patient to promote quality of life
(Resources 1, 2, 3, 4, 5).
Medical Management
Cytotoxic chemotherapy: all (Figures 2 and 3)
Local response may be particularly substantial in lymphoma and myeloma.
Hormone management: breast, prostate
Aromatase inhibitors or selective estrogen receptor modulators: breast
Androgen receptor blocking agents or androgen deprivation therapy: prostate
Growth factor receptor inhibitors: renal, lung
Diphosphonates (Figure 4)
Inhibit osteoclast activity by inducing apoptosis
Nitrogen-containing diphosphonates inhibit protein prenylation and guanosine
triphosphatase formation through osteoclast farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase enzyme
inhibition via the mevalonate pathway.
Nonnitrogen-containing diphosphonates induce osteoclasts to undergo apoptosis by forming
an adenosine triphosphate analogue.


Medical Management
Medical therapy for metastatic disease includes agents primarily targeted at slowing the
primary cancer process and bone-directed agents specifically for metastatic bone
disease.
Chemotherapy, hormone management, and receptor targeting medications are
administered primarily for the management of the primary cancer process; however,
they have the potential to promote reduction in metastatic lesion size and promote
healing in patients with a pathologic fracture. Certain histologies are more sensitive to
radiation therapy or systemic therapy than other histologies. Lymphoma, myeloma, and
breast cancer are histologies that may show drastic local response to and symptom
improvement from nonsurgical therapy. With the addition of antiresorptive therapy,
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:44 PM
AAOS | Metastatic Bone Disease
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004048
6/37

such as diphosphonates or receptor activator of nuclear factor-kappa B ligand inhibitors,
nonsurgical management of appropriately selected histologies may result in
reconstitution of bone stock without surgical management. This may have implications
on the need for or the extent of surgical management that may be required. Hormone
management is mostly used for breast cancer (aromatase inhibitors or selective
estrogen receptor modulators reduce estrogen production and slow the growth of
cancers that require estrogen) and prostate cancer (androgen receptor blocking agents
or androgen deprivation therapy). More recent medical therapies known as tyrosine
kinase inhibitors target specific growth factor receptors inherent to tumorigenesis, such
as vascular endothelial growth factor receptor in renal cell carcinoma and epidermal
growth factor receptor in lung carcinoma.1,2 Patients being treated with medication that
inhibits angiogenesis (such as anti–vascular endothelial growth factor receptor therapy)
must discontinue their medication preoperatively to decrease the risk of wound healing
complications.
Diphosphonates and denosumab are bone-targeting agents used in patients with
metastatic bone disease because of their ability to inhibit bone resorption and
subsequently reduce SREs, such as pathologic fracture, the need for radiation therapy or
surgical management of the bone, or spinal cord compression. Diphosphonates, such as
zoledronic acid, directly induce osteoclast apoptosis, whereas denosumab is a
monoclonal antibody that binds to osteoblast-produced receptor activator of nuclear
factor-kappa B ligand, which prevents activation of osteoclasts. A 2013 study reported
that zoledronic acid prolonged time to SRE in asymptomatic and symptomatic lesions;
however, its relative effect was greater in patients without pain at baseline.3
Diphosphonates also have demonstrated an analgesic effect that has synergistic
potential in combination with radiation therapy.4 In 2010, denosumab was approved for
use in patients with solid tumor bone metastases to prevent SREs. Overall, denosumab
has been shown to be superior to zoledronic acid in delaying time to first SRE in patients
with breast or prostate carcinoma and noninferior to zoledronic acid in patients with
non-breast/non-prostate metastatic bone disease; however, no difference has been
shown between the two agents in terms of survival or disease progression.5 A meta-
analysis of randomized trials of more than 7,000 patients in 2020 showed denosumab to
be moderately superior to zoledronic acid in reducing the likelihood of pathologic
fracture in patients with bone metastases; however, no difference was noted between
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:44 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004048
7/37

the two agents by specific cancer type.6 The current standard of care and the National
Comprehensive Cancer Network and the European Society for Medical Oncology
recommend that a diphosphonate or denosumab be administered to all patients with
metastatic bone disease and expected survival of more than 3 months who have
adequate renal function.7,8 Routine dental examinations are recommended for patients
being treated with either medication because of the rare but substantial adverse effect
of osteonecrosis of the jaw.9 Calcium and vitamin D supplementation also is
recommended to reduce the occurrence of hypocalcemia.10
Radiation Therapy
(Video 1)
External beam radiation therapy (EBRT)
Indications: pain, impending fracture, neurologic symptoms
Dose
30 Gy in 10 fractions or 20 Gy in 5 fractions are equivalent doses for bone lesions.
8 Gy in a single dose is effective for palliative pain relief; however, retreatment rates are
higher.
Some histologies (renal cell carcinoma) typically are more radioresistant, and higher,
hypofractionated dosing is described to improve local tumor control.

Pain relief in 70% of patients; however, this often takes 2 weeks.
Postoperatively, the surgical field and implant are irradiated after wound healing
(approximately 2 to 3 weeks) to theoretically decrease fixation failure and improve local

progression without instability or myelopathy.

Radiation therapy may predispose bone to fracture, which usually occurs approximately 1
year after radiation therapy.

Iodine 131 is used to manage metastatic thyroid cancer.

Radiation Therapy
Radiation therapy, or EBRT, is the main local treatment option for painful bone
metastasis. EBRT can be performed alone or in an adjuvant manner after surgical
management. For painful lesions that are deemed mechanically stable without
imminent risk of pathologic fracture, EBRT therapy alone often is the initial treatment.
The American Society for Radiation Oncology has shown that EBRT affords successful
pain palliation in 50% to 80% of patients, with one-third achieving complete pain
relief.11,12 Pain relief is more reliable in patients with multiple myeloma, breast, or
prostate cancer compared with patients with lung, renal cell, or thyroid cancer.13
Treatment regimens often are 30 Gy in 10 fractions or 20 Gy in 5 fractions, and pain
relief typically reaches maximum effect approximately 2 weeks after treatment
completion. Although pain relief is similar with multiple-fraction (30 Gy in 10 fractions)
or single-fraction (8 Gy in 1 fraction) management, the need for re-irradiation is
approximately two times higher in patients who undergo single-fraction treatment.14
A 2017 randomized controlled trial concluded that a single 8-Gy dose should be
offered to all patients with painful bone metastasis, even those with poor survival
because 40% of patients responded as early as 10 days after treatment.15 The use of
intravenous radionuclides, such as samarium or strontium chloride, which may
provide pain palliation and delay the progression of lesions is more common in
patients with multiple osteoblastic metastases.12,16 Specific to metastatic thyroid
cancer, radioactive iodine therapy in combination with resection of bone metastases
has been shown to be associated with improved survival and quality of life.17
Minimally Invasive Techniques

Creates an ice ball within lytic lesions
Radiofrequency ablation (Resource 7)
Thermal ablation to periosteal nerves at bone-tumor interface
Embolization (Resource 8)

Cementoplasty

Kyphoplasty/vertebroplasty (Figure 5)
Pain relief in patients with vertebral compression fractures from metastasis
The risk of cement leakage in vertebroplasty (35% to 65%) usually is not clinically relevant.
Vertebroplasty is not indicated for osteoporotic spine compression fractures; however, it is
used for metastatic disease and multiple myeloma affecting the spine.


Minimally Invasive Techniques
Over the past two decades, interventional procedures or minimally invasive techniques
have included rapidly evolving options for patients with painful bone metastases
refractory to prior management, patients who are not surgical candidates, and patients
with very limited prognosis (<3 months).18-21 Procedures are percutaneous
(radiofrequency ablation, cryoablation, cementoplasty, embolization) or noninvasive
(magnetic resonance–guided focused ultrasonography). These techniques often are
performed by interventional musculoskeletal radiologists under CT guidance and general
anesthesia; however, local anesthesia has been successfully used. The availability of
these procedures is institution dependent. In general, these procedures are best
indicated in patients with oligometastatic cancer who have well-defined osseous pain
from lytic or mixed metastatic lesions. The procedures have been performed in diverse
anatomic locations, including the pelvis, chest wall, spine, and almost all bones of the
upper and lower extremity. the procedures can be performed alone or in combination
with radiotherapy. Although most clinical outcome data is from retrospective case series,
all techniques have demonstrated promising pain relief—some achieving complete
relief, several months of relief, or relief as early as 24 hours after the procedure.22-26
Cryoablation involves the application of liquid nitrogen to create an ice-ball within the
bone lesion/cavity, which ideally has at least 75% coverage by thick walls or at least 1 cm
of subchondral bone from the lesion.27
Radiofrequency ablation causes thermal necrosis and destruction of periosteal nerves
and has been recommended for smaller tumors (<8 cm). The percentage of the bone-
tumor interface ablated (rather than the percentage of the overall tumor) directly
correlates with increased pain relief.28
Although commonly used in the neoadjuvant setting to limit intra-operative blood loss,
embolization has shown merit in pain palliation and tumor size reduction if used alone,
particularly in lesions of renal or thyroid origin.26

High-intensity focused ultrasonography is a newer, less available, extracorporeal
technique that does not involve the use of radiation therapy but rather ultrasonographic
energy to create thermal damage to painful adjacent periosteum.29 Smaller series with
less follow-up show promising clinical data; however, this technique, compared with the
other techniques presented, is less widely available, even at academic institutions.25
Extra-spinal cementoplasty has shown the best utility in weight-bearing bones (pelvis,
acetabulum, femur), possibly because of its mechanically stabilizing effect.23
In metastatic spine lesions, kyphoplasty and vertebroplasty have been shown to
substantially reduce pain and the need for opioid medications.30 Although bone cement
leakage is common, it often is asymptomatic.
Surgical Management
Goals of surgical management
Relieve pain
Improve function
Restore skeletal stability
Provide a construct with lifelong durability
Overview
To achieve these goals, several factors must be considered: namely, the functional status of the
patient and his or her bone quality. Typically, cement is used extensively in fixation techniques to
improve stability. In arthroplasty, cemented components tend to be the standard of care for
patients with metastatic disease.31 The overarching aim is to create a durable fixation construct
that will promote pain reduction and an acceptable functional outcome for the patient’s
remainder-of-life goals while outlasting the anticipated lifespan of the patient.
Indications
Indications for fixation: risk for fracture32 (Resource 10; Figure 6)

Indications
The radiographic appearance of a lesion refers to whether the metastatic disease is
blastic (1 point), mixed (2 points), or lytic (3 points). Size refers to the entire diameter of
the bone rather than solely the cortex, and the diameter of the bone is divided into
thirds: a lesion occupying less than one-third (1 point), between one-third and two-thirds
(2 points), and more than two-thirds (3 points) of the diameter of the bone. Site refers to
whether the lesion is in an upper extremity (1 point), lower extremity (2 points), or the
peritrochanteric region (3 points). Finally, pain is divided into nonfunctional (mild and
moderate pain, 1 and 2 points, respectively) and functional (3 points) pain. Functional
pain is suggestive of decreased mechanical strength of the bone, suggesting imminent
fracture.31,32
Prophylactic Fixation
Prophylactic fixation is recommended for patients with a Mirels score of 9 or higher (33%
fracture risk).

In the original study by Mirels,32 35% of the lesions fractured and 65% did not fracture.
In the patients without a fracture, Mirels scores ranged from 4 to 9; in the patients with a
fracture, Mirels scores ranged from 7 to 12. The risk of fracture for a Mirels score of 7
was 4%, with a 22% false-positive rate. This risk of fracture increased to 15% for a Mirels
score of 8, with a 6% false-positive rate. A Mirels score of 9 proved to be the most
accurate; the risk of fracture increased to 33%, with a false-positive rate of zero.
Mirels Classification
Mirels classification system frequently is used; however, its reliability is somewhat
questionable.

Mirels Classification
The reliability of Mirels criteria has been a subject of debate in various studies. Problems
with Mirels criteria include that the system does not consider the type of tumor or cell
biology. In addition, in the original study by Mirels,32 50 of the 78 lesions examined were
in patients with breast cancer. No patients with thyroid or renal cell carcinoma, two
malignancies that commonly metastasize to bone, were included in the study. Evans et
al33 specifically assessed humeral fractures. The authors found Mirels criteria to be
reproducible, valid, and more effective than clinical judgement alone but noted that the
overall specificity of the system is poor. With a cutoff Mirels score of 9 or greater for
femoral lesions and a Mirels score of 7 or greater for humeral lesions, the sensitivity was
80% to 90%; however, the specificity was 30% to 35%. Damron et al34 also noted overall
good sensitivity but poor specificity of the Mirels criteria. In examining femoral lesions,
the authors agreed that the criteria are more effective than clinical judgement alone and
reported a sensitivity of 91% and a specificity of 35%.

Harrington Criteria
An avulsion fracture of the lesser trochanter may be the first indicator of undiagnosed
metastatic bone disease. This type of fracture represents the normal pull of the iliopsoas
overcoming trochanteric metastatic disease, resulting in the avulsion, and may be
indicative of future intertrochanteric or subtrochanteric fracture.36,37

Harrington Classification of Acetabular Lesions
Surgical treatment typically is indicated in patients with extremely painful lesions or
lesions of the acetabular dome or the weight-bearing posterior column. The Harrington
classification of acetabular lesions typically aids in determining the type of surgical
treatment required.35,38

Van der Linden Criteria
Van der Linden et al39 reviewed a series of patients with femoral metastases who had
underwent radiation therapy and assessed those in whom a fracture lateral occurred.

The authors reviewed conventional risk factors, including increasing pain, lesion size
larger than 2.5 cm, radiographic osteolytic appearance, proximal location of the lesion, a
ratio of the width of the metastasis to the width of the bone greater than 0.6, transverse
cortical involvement, axial cortical involvement of more than 3.0 cm, and circumferential
involvement of more than 50%. The authors reported that axial cortical involvement of
more than 3.0 cm and circumferential involvement of more than 50% were the only
factors predictive of fracture. Axial cortical involvement of more than 3.0 cm was
associated with a negative predictive value (NPV) of 97%, a positive predictive value (PPV)
of 23%, and a specificity of 58%, whereas circumferential involvement of more than 50%
was associated with a NPV of 91%, a PPV of 26%, and a specificity of 82%.
Some surgeons note that CT scans are a more accurate method to determine fracture
risk than plain radiographs in patients with metastatic disease. CT-based structural
rigidity analysis (CTRA) has been suggested to be more sensitive and specific, with a
higher PPV and NPV, than Mirels criteria in predicting fracture. Damron et al40 found
that CTRA showing a reduction of more than 35% in axial, bending, or torsional rigidities
was associated with a lesion at high risk for fracture, with a sensitivity of 100%, specificity
of 60.6%, PPV of 17.6%, and NPV of 100% (compared with the Mirels criteria, which was
associated with a sensitivity, specificity, PPV, and NPV of 66.7%, 47.9%, 9.8%, and 94.4%,
respectively). Similarly, Nazarian et al41 reported a sensitivity of 100% and a specificity of
90% with CTRA compared with a sensitivity and specificity of 71% and 50%, respectively,
with the Mirels criteria. The limitation of CTRA is that it requires a CT scan, which may be
unavailable and/or considered unnecessary for many patients with metastatic lesions.
Spinal Lesions
Spinal lesions: impending fracture/collapse and neurologic changes

Spinal Lesions
Symptomatic spine lesions are more common in the thoracic spine (68% to 70%) than in
the lumbar spine (16% to 22%) and the cervical spine (15%).42 The reason the risk of
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:44 PM
AAOS | Metastatic Bone Disease
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004048
20/37

neurologic compromise is the greatest in the thoracic spine is that this area has the
smallest spinal canal to spinal cord size ratio. In addition, the blood supply to the spinal
cord is the most tenuous between the fourth and ninth thoracic vertebrae, making
vascular injury to the spinal cord more likely.43 Spinal instability that may require
surgical stabilization can be defined by lesions that include more than 50% vertebral
body collapse, tumor involvement of two or three columns, or involvement of a single
column at two or more spinal levels.37 Multiple studies have shown that surgical
treatment may be beneficial in patients with metastatic spine disease with regard to
pain, neurologic symptoms, and functionality.44,45 Various classification systems for
spinal lesions exist, including the Harrington classification of spinal lesions and the
Tomita prognostic scoring system.43,46
Other Factors To Consider
Scoring systems are not exact and cannot predict all human factors.
Histology of the primary lesion
Expected lifespan, comorbid conditions, and activity level of the patient
Most surgical decisions can be based on plain radiographs (MRI not necessary in patients with
extremity lesions)
Prophylactic fixation compared with fixation of actual pathologic fracture:
Decreased perioperative morbidity/pain
Shorter surgical time
Faster recovery/shorter hospital length of stay
Ability to coordinate care with medical oncology

Other Factors To Consider
Current oncologic status and prognosis must be considered and discussed with the
patient. A patient’s other medical comorbidities and expected life span must be
considered in discussing surgical treatment. A patient with a declining medical status
and a short life expectancy (eg, <4 weeks) may not be able to tolerate surgical treatment.

In these scenarios, minimally invasive or noninterventional palliative techniques are
more appropriate. A good patient history must be obtained and a physical examination
must be performed to determine a patient’s level of function. Radiographs of the entire
involved bone must be obtained to evaluate for skip lesions; often, advanced imaging
studies are not required unless a large soft-tissue mass is anticipated and may alter
surgical technique.37,47
Performing prophylactic fixation of an impending fracture is technically easier than
surgically reducing, fixing, and healing a fracture. Healing of a fractured bone is difficult
in a patient who is undergoing chemotherapy or radiation therapy. Clinically, patients
also have better functional outcomes with prophylactic fixation. Ward et al48 found that
patients who underwent prophylactic fixation had shorter hospital length of stays and a
higher likelihood to be discharged to home rather than to a nursing facility compared
with patients who underwent treatment for an existing pathologic fracture. In a
retrospective comparative study, Aneja et al49 found that patients who underwent
prophylactic fixation had a substantially lower rate of postoperative urinary tract
infections and blood transfusions and were more likely to be discharged to home when
compared with patients who underwent pathologic fracture fixation; however, the
authors reported a considerably higher rate of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary
embolism in the prophylactic fixation group compared with the fracture fixation group.

Histology is an important factor to consider in selecting the optimal treatment option for
metastatic bone disease. Although lymphoma, myeloma, breast, and prostate cancer
respond quite well to radiation therapy, histologies such as thyroid, lung, and renal cell
carcinoma are much more resistant in terms of a complete response. Pain relief can be
achieved in patients with renal or thyroid cancer; however, patients with these types of
bony metastases may respond better overall to surgical treatment.13,50 Thyroid and

should be considered, especially in patients with lesions in the pelvis. Preoperative

Economic Considerations
The economic burden of metastatic bone disease in the United States was estimated to
be almost $13 billion in 2007 and approximately 17% of the overall cost burden in
oncology care.55 With improving systemic treatment options in the past decade, the
number of patients living with metastatic bone disease is increasing and is expected to
continue to increase.
A common clinical scenario for orthopaedic surgeons treating patients with metastatic
bone disease is impending pathologic fractures. Classification systems aid in determining
appropriate management. Pathologic fractures are associated with a worse health
burden on the patient: pathologic fractures are associated with poorer survival in almost
all subtypes, with the greatest increased risk of death in patients with breast cancer
(approximately 30%).56 According to national registry data, prophylactic fixation of
impending fractures is associated with decreased complications, decreased hospital
length of stay, and faster postoperative rehabilitation compared with acute fixation of
pathologic fractures.57 In addition, prophylactic management of impending fractures has
been shown to be associated with lower overall costs (more than 40%).57,58 Given the
combined health and financial merit of prophylactic fixation over acute fixation, early
and safe surgical management is supported for impending fractures from metastatic
bone disease.
A clear path of communication between physicians and patients with regard to
symptoms and monitoring metastatic bone lesions is the best method for determining
the appropriate timing of management.
